title: Financial Markets: Where Savings Meet Borrowers

questions.question: Financial markets essentially channel funds from:
questions.rationale: Households save more than they invest; firms and government invest more than they save — markets and intermediaries bridge the two.

questions.question: In an IPO, the money paid for shares goes to:
options: The selling shareholders or the company in the primary market
questions.rationale: An IPO is a primary-market issue — the company (or offer-for-sale shareholders) receives the proceeds; afterwards, secondary trading pays only the selling investor.

questions.question: Market interest rates rise from 8% to 10%. The price of an existing 8%-coupon bond will:
questions.rationale: New bonds pay more, so old bonds must become cheaper to compete — bond prices and yields always move in opposite directions.

questions.question: Which is India's oldest stock exchange (established 1875)?
questions.rationale: The Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) dates to 1875 — Asia's first; NSE began electronic screen-based trading in 1994.

questions.question: A mutual fund's NAV represents:
questions.rationale: Net Asset Value is the per-unit worth of the fund's portfolio; SIPs buy units at each instalment's NAV, averaging cost over time.

questions.question: SEBI's statutory objectives are to:
options: Protect investors, develop the securities market, and regulate it
questions.rationale: The SEBI Act 1992 gives the triple mandate — investor protection, market development, market regulation — via IPO disclosure norms, insider-trading rules, and surveillance.

questions.question: Which regulator supervises the money market and government securities?
questions.rationale: The RBI regulates banks, the money market (T-bills, call money, commercial paper), G-secs, payments, and forex; SEBI handles the securities market.

questions.question: A stock index like NIFTY 50 is weighted by:
questions.rationale: Larger free-float market caps move the index more — free float excludes promoter-held shares unavailable for trading.

questions.question: An option gives its buyer:
options: The right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price
questions.rationale: Options convey a right exercisable at choice (hence the premium paid); futures impose a binding obligation on both parties.

questions.question: Which of these shows the power of compounding?
options: ₹10,000 invested yearly for 30 years at 12% grows to roughly ₹1.4 crore
questions.rationale: Compounding converts steady SIPs into large sums over decades — the arithmetic case for starting early rather than timing markets.
